notes:
Here are my notes on Luke 22:48–71. I ran out of search and fetch calls, so most of these come from search-result excerpts rather than full pages. I couldn't fully open the Enduring Word section on these verses, and I didn't reach netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, or any prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace sources, so those views are missing. A few verses (55, 63–65) have little material.

**v. 48**
- Judas greeted Jesus with the usual kiss, but the kiss's real job was to point Jesus out to the arresting party. Guzik says Jesus' question amounts to asking whether Judas was so numb that he could kiss and betray at once, and calls Judas an example of a seared conscience. Judas warmly greeted Jesus, even giving Him the customary kiss. But the kiss only precisely identified Jesus to the authorities  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Guzik quotes Barclay: this was how a disciple greeted a beloved rabbi, which makes the betrayal worse. It was the kiss of a disciple to a beloved master that Judas used as a sign of betrayal. — same URL
- The Pulpit Commentary says the kiss was the agreed signal, and calls the betrayal "the semblance of friendship." This was the sign agreed upon between Judas and his employers.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-22.html
- Matthew Henry: the crowd didn't know where to find Jesus or which man he was, and Judas solved both problems by using the closeness Jesus had allowed his disciples.  — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
- Deffinbaugh (bible.org): Luke focuses on what Jesus said and did, not on what was done to him. Jesus rebukes three times and heals once. Rebuking Judas is the first of these.  — https://bible.org/seriespage/71-rejection-israels-messiah-part-i-luke-2247-71

**v. 49**
- Quoting Blum, Precept Austin calls Peter's loyalty touching but blind to God's plan, a case of zeal without knowledge (Rom 10:2). Stein adds that the disciples hadn't prayed, so they neither understood nor could act rightly in the crisis. "Peter's blind loyalty was touching, but it missed God's plan. Zeal without knowledge in religion often leads men astray (cf. Ro 10:2)."  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary

**v. 50**
- Coffman: John 18:10 names the servant as Malchus, and Luke, as a physician, notes that it was the right ear.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-51.html

**v. 51** (Protestant writers explain this verse in noticeably different ways)
- *The wording is unclear.* The Greek is a short, everyday phrase whose sense may have depended on tone or gesture. It could mean "leave me free to heal this man" (to the captors), "let them arrest me" (to the disciples), or "no more weapons." The Expositor's Greek Testament leans toward "stop, that's enough," said to the disciples. The Pulpit Commentary thinks it was said to the soldiers, asking pardon for Peter ("excuse this resistance"). Vincent reads it as an answer to the disciples.    — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/22-51.htm
- *Wesleyan (Adam Clarke):* he takes it as "let me go this far," meaning Jesus asked the captors to let him reach Malchus and heal him.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-51.html
- *Reformed (Calvin):* Peter's rash zeal shamed Christ and his teaching. Calvin sees Satan trying to make Christ look like the leader of armed rebels, and thinks that is why Jesus healed the wound.  — same URL
- *Baptist (Gill):* the healing shows Christ still had power to do miracles even in his humbled state. It also showed his kindness to enemies and proved he went willingly, since someone who could do this could easily have escaped.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/22-51.htm
- *Dispensational evangelical (Constable):* Jesus rebuked Peter rather than asking the soldiers' permission. He did good to his enemies, as he had taught, and did not build his kingdom on force.   — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-51.html
- *MacArthur (gty.org):* the strongest application. He says there is no legitimate Christian revolt and God's cause is not advanced by the sword. He also notes this is the only New Testament example of an open wound healed instantly, with no faith required.   — https://www.gty.org/sermons/42-274/a-traitorous-kiss-for-the-triumphant-savior
- *Practical reasons:* Coffman and Gann (Restoration Movement) say the healing protected the disciples, because Peter's act could otherwise have got them arrested. The BibleHub notes agree that it removed any legal excuse to arrest them, so Jesus alone would bear the judgment.   — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-51.html  — https://biblehub.com/luke/22-51.htm
- The BibleHub notes say only Luke records this last public healing before the cross, and see in it a picture of the atonement (Isa 53:5).   — https://biblehub.com/luke/22-51.htm

**vv. 52–53**
- Deffinbaugh: Jesus had taught openly in the temple every day. They chose to seize him secretly at night, under cover of darkness and deceit (the kiss, for example).  — https://bible.org/seriespage/71-rejection-israels-messiah-part-i-luke-2247-71
- BibleHub's overview: the arrest was led by temple police, not Roman soldiers (John 18 adds that Romans joined), and Jesus exposes their cowardice in verse 53.  — https://biblehub.com/luke/22.htm

**v. 54**
- Guzik: Peter cared enough to follow but lacked the courage to be openly linked with Jesus, and the distance made confessing him harder. The other disciples ran, while Peter hoped to prove Jesus' prediction wrong.   — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Pulpit Commentary on fitting the Gospels together: Jesus was questioned first before Annas (John 18), then before Caiaphas with a committee of the Sanhedrin, and then formally before the full Sanhedrin at dawn.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-22.html

**v. 55**
- BibleHub notes that excavations have uncovered first-century priestly houses with fire pits, matching this scene.  — https://biblehub.com/luke/22.htm

**vv. 56–60**
- Guzik sees three steps down: Peter denies knowing Jesus, then denies being his follower, then denies even being from Galilee.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Utley (bible.org): "know" carries its Hebrew sense, so Peter is denying any personal relationship with Jesus. In verse 58 he denies being a disciple. In verse 59 the giveaway is his accent, and he even denies that.  — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-22
- Pulpit: Peter thought he could face anything for Jesus and would have laughed at the idea that a servant girl's sneer could break him. His temptation was to stay linked to what looked like a lost cause.   — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-22.html
- Matthew Henry: Peter had neither the courage to admit it nor the presence of mind to sidestep it, and one lie makes the next easier.   — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
- Spurgeon (v. 60) points to the other Gospels, which say Peter began to curse and swear, as if that were the best proof he didn't know Jesus.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke
- Deffinbaugh thinks Peter didn't realise he was fulfilling Jesus' prediction until after the third denial.  — https://bible.org/seriespage/71-rejection-israels-messiah-part-i-luke-2247-71

**v. 61**
- Only Luke records Jesus' look. Maclaren says Luke shows two things working together, the rooster and the look.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/22-61.htm
- Matthew Henry calls it a look of compassion that also carried grace into Peter's heart so he could repent. Gill calls it a look of love and mercy, not anger.    — same URL
- Guzik: the look convicted Peter of both the denial and the pride that made him think he could never fall.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Precept Austin cites the point that Christ's look did not move the chief priests as it moved Peter. What restored Peter was the divine grace that came with it.  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary
- The BibleHub Study Bible sees the Holy Spirit's work in bringing Jesus' words back to Peter's mind.  — https://biblehub.com/study/luke/22-61.htm

**v. 62**
- Peter versus Judas. Maclaren says Judas saw his sin only through an awakened conscience and despaired, while Peter saw it in the face of a forgiving Lord. MacArthur says Peter's remorse became repentance, while Judas's became suicide.  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/22-61.htm  — https://www.gty.org/sermons/43-102/jesus-unjust-trial-peters-shameful-denial
- R.C. Sproul (Reformed) stresses how deep the grief was, and that it ended in tears, not suicide.  — https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/peters-denial-luke
- Guzik links this to verse 32 ("that your faith should not fail"): Peter fell but did not fall away.  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Andrew Murray (Holiness/Keswick devotional writer): Peter had left his nets but not his old self. He had to be humbled before Christ could fill him with the Spirit.   — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/murray_andrew/surrender/surrender04.cfm
- *Catholic and Orthodox (older Fathers):* in Aquinas's Catena Aurea, Bede says Peter washed away his denial with tears of penance. Theophylact uses Peter against the Novatians, who denied forgiveness for sins committed after baptism: Peter had received the Lord's body and blood and was still restored through penitence. Note that this comes from the Catena on *Mark's* account, not Luke's.   — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena2.iii.xiv.html

**vv. 63–65**
- The irony: they mocked Jesus' gift of prophecy just after his prophecy about Peter had come true (quoted by Guzik).  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Pulpit: this mocking happened while they waited for the full council to gather.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-22.html
- Precept Austin lists beating the prisoner among the laws broken, and quotes Fruchtenbaum calling this stage a complete travesty of Jewish justice.   — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary

**v. 66**
- Pulpit: the council couldn't legally meet until dawn, which explains the timing.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-22.html
- Precept Austin lists other rules broken: the verdict was given the same day, and the trial was held on the eve of a feast.   — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-22-commentary

**vv. 67–68**
- Utley: the council wanted to condemn Jesus, not learn about him. Their hearts were already hard, and he goes as far as saying the unpardonable sin had already happened. That last claim is his own; the other sources don't make it.   — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-22
- Kelly: asking "Are you the Christ?" came too late, because they had already shown they would not believe.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-70.html

**v. 69**
- Constable: Jesus claimed a unique closeness to God, which counted as blasphemy. "Son of Man" echoes Daniel 7:13–14, and the verse implies the Messiah would not reign right away.   — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-70.html
- Matthew Henry: Jesus points them to his future glory as the full proof. Barclay: even after a night of abuse, Jesus was completely sure of his triumph. Kelly: Luke's "from now on" refers to something close at hand, not only to a distant future.    — same URL
- BibleHub notes the echoes of Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13–14.  — https://biblehub.com/luke/22-70.htm
- John Piper (desiringgod.org), preaching on Matthew's parallel, describes a reversal: the man now on trial will be seated as judge.  — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/you-will-see-the-son-of-man-seated-at-the-right-hand-of-power-and-coming-on-the-clouds-of-heaven

**v. 70**
- Most read "You say that I am" as a yes. Gill takes it as "you say it, and rightly, for I am." Coffman calls it the strongest affirmation and says reading it as anything less is a gross error. Ellicott says it implies a confession, as Matthew and Mark make clearer.   — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-70.html  — https://biblehub.com/luke/22-70.htm
- Utley cites Moffatt's paraphrase: "That is your word, not mine, I would not put it like that, but since you have, I cannot deny it."  — https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-22
- The BibleHub Study Bible gives a slightly different reading. Jesus accepts their words without making a claim that could be used against him legally, and it hears an echo of "I AM" in Exodus 3:14.   — https://biblehub.com/study/luke/22-70.htm

**v. 71**
- Kelly: Jesus admits the truth, and they need nothing more to condemn him.  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-70.html
- BibleHub: the council couldn't carry out executions under Rome, so it needed a capital charge. The question may have been a deliberate attempt to get Jesus to incriminate himself.  — https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Sanhedrin_ask_Jesus_in_Luke_22_70.htm
